subtopics.name: Photoelectric Effect

step_list: Write Einstein's equation for the first light: e(V_s/2) = h(ν − ν₀).
Write it for the second light: eV_s = h(ν/2 − ν₀).
Eliminate V_s (double the first equation and equate) and solve the linear relation for ν₀.
difficulty.why: Three short steps of standard photoelectric algebra, but the deciding work is entirely in handling the two factors of 2 — one on the frequency and one on the stopping potential — and two of the distractors sit exactly where those factors get mishandled, so elimination by plausibility does nothing.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The stem deliberately pairs the higher frequency with the SMALLER stopping potential, which looks physically backwards and tempts candidates to 'fix' the assignment before solving; combined with the dropped-factor-of-two options, a correct method still reaches a wrong key.

spec.title: P-V diagram: four processes from a common initial state — isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic, isochoric

steps: Curve $1$ is vertical ($V$ constant), so it is isochoric.
Curve $4$ is horizontal ($P$ constant), so it is isobaric.
For the isothermal process $PV = \text{const}$, so $\frac{dP}{dV} = -\frac{P}{V}$.
For the adiabatic process $PV^{\gamma} = \text{const}$, so $\frac{dP}{dV} = -\gamma\frac{P}{V}$.
Since $\gamma > 1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one from the same initial state.
Curve $2$ is steeper than curve $3$, so curve $2$ is adiabatic, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. Curve 1 is vertical (V constant), so it is isochoric.
  2. Curve 4 is horizontal (P constant), so it is isobaric.
  3. For the isothermal process PV = const, so dPdV = -PV.
  4. For the adiabatic process PVγ = const, so dPdV = -γPV.
  5. Since γ > 1, the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal one from the same initial state.
  6. Curve 2 is steeper than curve 3, so curve 2 is adiabatic, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Curve 1 is vertical (isochoric), 4 horizontal (isobaric); of the two falling curves the steeper one (3) is adiabatic since its slope is gamma times the isothermal slope.

chapter.name: Thermodynamics
chapter.why: The answer depends on recognising that the adiabatic P–V curve is steeper than the isothermal one among the four thermodynamic processes shown.

subtopics.name: Adiabatic Process
subtopics.why: The answer depends on the adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram being steeper than the isothermal curve (slope -gamma P/V versus -P/V), a property of the adiabatic process.

step_list: Recognise the vertical line 1 as isochoric and the horizontal line 4 as isobaric, leaving curves 2 and 3 as the isothermal/adiabatic pair
Apply |dP/dV|_adiabatic = γ × |dP/dV|_isothermal, so the steeper falling curve (2) is the adiabat
difficulty.why: Medium: the first step throws away half the options on sight, but the remaining choice between the two hyperbola-like curves turns entirely on remembering that the adiabat is the steeper of the pair — a candidate who mixes that up lands squarely on option 4.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The single recalled relation (adiabatic slope = γ × isothermal slope) is the only thing separating the two live curves, and the commonest error is reversing it.

steps: In circuit (a) both junctions are oriented $P\to N$ in series, so the same current flows through both with the same bias; identical junctions give $V_1 = V_2$.
In circuit (b) one junction is $P\to N$ and the other $N\to P$, so one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; $V_{\text{forward}} \ll V_{\text{reverse}}$, so the drops are unequal.
In circuit (c) both junctions are oriented $N\to P$ in series, so both have the same bias and $V_1 = V_2$.
Equal drops occur in (a) and (c), which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In circuit (a) both junctions are oriented P→ N in series, so the same current flows through both with the same bias; identical junctions give V1 = V2.
  2. In circuit (b) one junction is P→ N and the other N→ P, so one is forward biased and the other reverse biased; Vforward ≪ Vreverse, so the drops are unequal.
  3. In circuit (c) both junctions are oriented N→ P in series, so both have the same bias and V1 = V2.
  4. Equal drops occur in (a) and (c), which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: In (a) and (c) both junctions face the same way in series, so both are equally forward (or reverse) biased and the drops are equal; in (b) one is forward and one reverse biased, so the drops differ.

chapter.name: Semiconductor Electronics
chapter.why: The answer depends on how the applied voltage divides between two p-n junctions depending on whether each is forward or reverse biased (symmetric arrangements give equal drops).

subtopics.name: PN Junction Diode Under Forward Bias
subtopics.why: The answer depends on recognising that the two series diodes are both identically biased in circuits (a) and (c) but one forward- and one reverse-biased in circuit (b), so the drops are equal only when both share the same bias state.

subtopics.name: PN Junction Diode Under Reverse Bias
subtopics.why: Circuit (b) joins a PN and an NP junction in series, so one is reverse-biased and takes almost the whole drop, and ruling (b) out depends on that reverse-bias behaviour.

step_list: Notice that (a) and (c) are the same circuit mirrored (both diodes pointing the same way round the loop), so they must stand or fall together — options (2) and (4) die immediately.
Trace the loop in (a)/(c): both junctions face the same way relative to the battery, so both are forward biased (or both reverse) and carry identical drops.
Trace (b): the two diodes are back-to-back, so one is reverse biased and takes almost the entire supply voltage while the other takes ~0.7 V — drops unequal.
difficulty.why: Medium: the symmetry argument kills two options on sight, so the question collapses to a single binary choice, but that choice needs the real physics — that identically oriented diodes share the drop equally while an opposed pair has one element reverse biased hogging nearly all of it — and the geometrically symmetric circuit (b) is exactly the wrong answer a careless candidate reaches for.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The visual symmetry of circuit (b) points the opposite way from the electrical answer; the candidate must trace bias direction around the loop rather than judge by appearance.

question.full_text:
When light propagates through a material medium of relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ and relative permeability $\mu_r$, the velocity of light, $v$ is given by ($c$-velocity of light in vacuum)
(1) $v = \dfrac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$
(2) $v = c$
(3) $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mu_r}{\varepsilon_r}}$
(4) $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{\varepsilon_r}{\mu_r}}$
question.html:
When light propagates through a material medium of relative permittivity εr and relative permeability μr, the velocity of light, v is given by (c-velocity of light in vacuum)
  1. (1)v = cεr μr
  2. (2)v = c
  3. (3)v = μrεr
  4. (4)v = εrμr
question.stem: When light propagates through a material medium of relative permittivity $\varepsilon_r$ and relative permeability $\mu_r$, the velocity of light, $v$ is given by ($c$-velocity of light in vacuum)

solution.full_text:
1. $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_m \mu_m}}$
2. $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mu_0 \mu_r}}$
3. Since $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \mu_0}}$
4. $\Rightarrow v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$
solution.html:
1. v = 1εm μm
  2. v = 1ε0 εr μ0 μr
  3. Since c = 1ε0 μ0
  4. ⇒ v = cεr μr
steps: $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_m \mu_m}}$
$v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \mu_0 \mu_r}}$
Since $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \mu_0}}$
$\Rightarrow v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$
In a medium, $v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu \varepsilon}}$ with $\mu = \mu_0 \mu_r$ and $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r$.
$v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_r \varepsilon_r}}$.
Since $c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$, $v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r}}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In a medium, v = 1μ ε with μ = μ0 μr and ε = ε0 εr.
  2. v = 1μ0 ε0 · 1μr εr.
  3. Since c = 1μ0 ε0, v = cεr μr, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: v = 1/sqrt(mu epsilon) = 1/sqrt(mu0 mu_r eps0 eps_r) = c/sqrt(eps_r mu_r).

The angle between the electric lines of force and the equipotential surface is

  2. (2)0°
  3. (3)45°
  4. (4)90°
question.stem: The angle between the electric lines of force and the equipotential surface is

solution.full_text:
1. $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$
2. $dV = -E\,dr\cos\theta$
3. For equipotential surface,
4. $dV = 0$
5. $\cos\theta = 0$
6. $\Rightarrow \theta = 90^\circ$
solution.html:
1. dV = -→E· d→r
  2. dV = -E drcosθ
  3. For equipotential surface,
  4. dV = 0
  5. cosθ = 0
  6. ⇒ θ = 90°
steps: $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{r}$
$dV = -E\,dr\cos\theta$
For equipotential surface,
$\cos\theta = 0$
$\Rightarrow \theta = 90^\circ$
Along an equipotential surface $dV = -\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$, so $\vec{E} \perp d\vec{l}$ and the lines of force meet the surface at $90^\circ$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html: 1. Along an equipotential surface dV = -→E· d→l = 0, so →E ⊥ d→l and the lines of force meet the surface at 90°, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: No work is done moving along an equipotential surface, so the field (lines of force) must be perpendicular to it: 90 degrees.

step_list: Recall that no work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface, so E must have no component along it — the field lines meet it perpendicularly.
difficulty.why: Easy: a single one-line NCERT fact with no calculation, and two of the four options (45°, 180°) are not statements anyone has ever made about equipotentials, so the choice collapses to perpendicular-versus-parallel, which every candidate has drawn in the field-line diagrams.

If the wavelength of light is changed to $400\,\mathrm{nm}$, then the number of fringes he would observe in the same region of the screen is
(1) 12
(2) 6
(3) 8
(4) 9

  1. (1)12
  2. (2)6
  3. (3)8
  4. (4)9
question.stem: In a Young's double slit experiment, a student observes 8 fringes in a certain segment of screen when a monochromatic light of $600\,\mathrm{nm}$ wavelength is used. If the wavelength of light is changed to $400\,\mathrm{nm}$, then the number of fringes he would observe in the same region of the screen is

solution.full_text:
1. $\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$
2. Let length of segment of screen $= l$
3. $\Rightarrow l = 8\beta_1 = \frac{8\lambda_1 D}{d}$ \quad ...(1)
4. and $l = n\beta_2 = \frac{n\lambda_2 D}{d}$ \quad ...(2)
5. from (1) and (2)
6. $8\lambda_1 = n\lambda_2$
7. $8(600\,\mathrm{nm}) = n(400\,\mathrm{nm})$
8. $n = 12$
solution.html:
1. β = λ Dd
  2. Let length of segment of screen = l
  3. ⇒ l = 8β1 = 8λ1 Dd     ...(1)
  4. and l = nβ2 = nλ2 Dd     ...(2)
  5. from (1) and (2)
  6. 8λ1 = nλ2

steps: The ball is dropped, so $v(0) = 0$, which rules out curves $C$ and $D$ because they do not start at $v=0$.
Net force: $m\frac{dv}{dt} = mg - F_B - 6\pi\eta r v$, so the acceleration falls as $v$ grows.
Solving gives $v = v_t\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$, which rises from zero and levels off at the terminal velocity $v_t$.
Curve $A$ is a straight line that keeps rising, so it has no terminal velocity. Curve $B$ rises and saturates, so the answer is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. Net force: mdvdt = mg - FB - 6πη r v, so the acceleration falls as v grows.
  3. Solving gives v = vt(1 - e-t/τ), which rises from zero and levels off at the terminal velocity vt.
  4. Curve A is a straight line that keeps rising, so it has no terminal velocity. Curve B rises and saturates, so the answer is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Dropped from rest, the ball speeds up while viscous drag grows with v, so v rises from zero and levels off at terminal velocity, which is curve B.

steps: For a conductor, $\rho_T = \rho_0[1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]$ with $\alpha > 0$, so resistance increases with temperature.

question.stem: Two resistors of resistance, $100\,\Omega$ and $200\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel in an electrical circuit. The ratio of the thermal energy developed in $100\,\Omega$ to that in $200\,\Omega$ in a given time is

solution.full_text:
1. For parallel combination
2. $P = \frac{V^{2}}{R}$
3. $\frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{R_2}{R_1}$
4. $\Rightarrow \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{200}{100} = \frac{2}{1}$
solution.html:
1. For parallel combination
  2. P = V2R
  3. P1P2 = R2R1
  4. ⇒ P1P2 = 200100 = 21
steps: For parallel combination
$\Rightarrow \frac{P_1}{P_2} = \frac{200}{100} = \frac{2}{1}$
In a parallel connection both resistors have the same potential difference $V$.
Heat developed in time $t$ is $H = \frac{V^2 t}{R}$, so $H \propto \frac{1}{R}$.
$\frac{H_{100}}{H_{200}} = \frac{200\,\Omega}{100\,\Omega} = \frac{2}{1}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. In a parallel connection both resistors have the same potential difference V.
  2. Heat developed in time t is H = V2 tR, so H ∝ 1R.
  3. H100H200 = 200 Ω100 Ω = 21, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: In parallel, V is the same, so H = V^2 t / R is inversely proportional to R: H100:H200 = 200:100 = 2:1.

2. $B = \mu_0 \frac{N}{\ell} I = \mu_0 n I$ $\qquad \left[n = \frac{N}{\ell}\right]$

4. $= 4\pi \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}$

  2. B = μ0 Nℓ I = μ0 n I    [n = Nℓ]
  3. = 4π × 10-7 × 100 × 103 × 1    [n = 10010-3]
  4. = 4π × 10-2 T
  5. B = 12.56 × 10-2 T

question.stem: A copper wire of length $10\,\mathrm{m}$ and radius $\left(\dfrac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)\,\mathrm{m}$ has electrical resistance of $10\,\Omega$. The current density in the wire for an electric field strength of $10\,(\mathrm{V/m})$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Resistance, $R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = \frac{L}{\sigma A}$
2. $\Rightarrow\ \sigma = \frac{L}{RA}$
3. Also current density $j = \sigma E = \frac{LE}{RA}$
4. $j = \frac{10\times 10}{10\times\pi\left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}} = \frac{100}{10\times\pi\times\left(\frac{10^{-4}}{\pi}\right)}$
5. $= 10^{5}\,\mathrm{A/m^{2}}$
solution.html:
1. Resistance, R = ρLA = Lσ A
  2. ⇒ σ = LRA
  3. Also current density j = σ E = LERA
  4. j = 10× 1010×π(10-2π)2 = 10010×π×(10-4π)
  5. = 105 A/m2
steps: Resistance, $R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = \frac{L}{\sigma A}$
$\Rightarrow\ \sigma = \frac{L}{RA}$
Also current density $j = \sigma E = \frac{LE}{RA}$
$j = \frac{10\times 10}{10\times\pi\left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{2}} = \frac{100}{10\times\pi\times\left(\frac{10^{-4}}{\pi}\right)}$
$A = \pi r^2 = \pi \left(\frac{10^{-2}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$.
$\rho = \frac{RA}{l} = \frac{10 \times 10^{-4}}{10} = 10^{-4}\,\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$.
$J = \frac{E}{\rho} = \frac{10}{10^{-4}} = 10^{5}\,\mathrm{A/m^2}$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. A = π r2 = π (10-2π)2 = 10-4 m2.
  2. ρ = RAl = 10 × 10-410 = 10-4 Ω m.
  3. J = Eρ = 1010-4 = 105 A/m2, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: A = pi r^2 = 1e-4 m^2, rho = RA/l = 1e-4 ohm m, J = E/rho = 10/1e-4 = 1e5 A/m^2.

solution.full_text:
1. Momentum of the system would remain conserved.
2. Initial momentum $= 0$
3. Final momentum should also be zero.
4. Let masses be $2m$, $2m$, and $m$
5. Momentum along $x$-direction $= 2mv\hat{i}$
6. Momentum along $y$-direction $= 2mv\hat{j}$
7. Net momentum $= \sqrt{(2mv)^2 + (2mv)^2} = \sqrt{2}\cdot 2mv$
8. Now, $2\sqrt{2}mv = mv'$
9. $v' = 2\sqrt{2}v$

question.html:

question.stem: The angular speed of a fly wheel moving with uniform angular acceleration changes from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 seconds. The angular acceleration in $\mathrm{rad/s^2}$ is

solution.full_text:
1. Angular acceleration $\alpha = \frac{\omega_f - \omega_i}{t}$
2. $\omega_f = 3120 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$ rad/s
3. $\omega_i = 1200 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$ rad/s
4. $\Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{(3120 - 1200)}{16} \times \frac{2\pi}{60} = 4\pi$
solution.html:
1. Angular acceleration α = ωf - ωit
  2. ωf = 3120 × 2π60 rad/s
  3. ωi = 1200 × 2π60 rad/s
  4. ⇒ α = (3120 - 1200)16 × 2π60 = 4π
steps: Angular acceleration $\alpha = \frac{\omega_f - \omega_i}{t}$
$\omega_f = 3120 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$ rad/s
$\omega_i = 1200 \times \frac{2\pi}{60}$ rad/s
$\Rightarrow \alpha = \frac{(3120 - 1200)}{16} \times \frac{2\pi}{60} = 4\pi$
Change in angular speed: $\Delta n = 3120 - 1200 = 1920\,\mathrm{rpm}$.
Convert to rev/s: $\frac{1920}{60} = 32\,\mathrm{rev/s}$.
Convert to rad/s: $\Delta\omega = 2\pi \times 32 = 64\pi\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$\alpha = \frac{\Delta\omega}{t} = \frac{64\pi}{16} = 4\pi\,\mathrm{rad/s^2}$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:

  2. Convert to rev/s: 192060 = 32 rev/s.
  3. Convert to rad/s: Δω = 2π × 32 = 64π rad/s.
  4. α = Δωt = 64π16 = 4π rad/s2, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Change in speed 1920 rpm = 32 rev/s = 64π rad/s over 16 s gives α = 4π rad/s^2.

(2) $1 : 1$
(3) $\sqrt{2} : 1$
(4) $1 : \sqrt{2}$

If the initial tension on a stretched string is doubled, then the ratio of the initial and final speeds of a transverse wave along the string is

  2. (2)1 : 1
  3. (3)2 : 1
  4. (4)1 : 2

2. $v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$
3. $\therefore\; v_i = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ and $v_f = \sqrt{\frac{2T}{\mu}}$
4. $\therefore\; \frac{v_i}{v_f} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

steps: For a thin uniform disc about the axis through the centre normal to its plane, $I_1 = \frac{MR^2}{2}$, so $k_1 = \sqrt{\frac{I_1}{M}} = \frac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$.
By the perpendicular axis theorem, $I_1 = 2I_d$, so $I_d = \frac{MR^2}{4}$.
Hence $k_2 = \sqrt{\frac{I_d}{M}} = \frac{R}{2}$.
$\frac{k_1}{k_2} = \frac{R/\sqrt{2}}{R/2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{2}$, so the ratio is $\sqrt{2}:1$, which is option $3$.
ai_solution.html:
1. For a thin uniform disc about the axis through the centre normal to its plane, I1 = MR22, so k1 = I1M = R2.
  2. By the perpendicular axis theorem, I1 = 2Id, so Id = MR24.
  3. Hence k2 = IdM = R2.
  4. k1k2 = R/2R/2 = 22 = 2, so the ratio is 2:1, which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: k_normal = R/sqrt2 (I = MR^2/2), k_diameter = R/2 (I = MR^2/4), so ratio = sqrt2 : 1.

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The word 'radius of gyration' rather than 'moment of inertia' is the hinge; the ratio-of-I distractor (2:1) is the most attractive wrong answer in the set, and the reversed-order distractor punishes misreading which axis comes first.

question.full_text:
A light ray falls on a glass surface of refractive index $\sqrt{3}$ , at an angle $60^\circ$. The angle between the refracted and reflected rays would be
(1) $120^\circ$
(2) $30^\circ$
(3) $60^\circ$
(4) $90^\circ$
question.html:
A light ray falls on a glass surface of refractive index 3 , at an angle 60°. The angle between the refracted and reflected rays would be
  1. (1)120°
  2. (2)30°
  3. (3)60°
  4. (4)90°
question.stem: A light ray falls on a glass surface of refractive index $\sqrt{3}$ , at an angle $60^\circ$. The angle between the refracted and reflected rays would be

solution.full_text:
1. Given $i = 60^\circ$ and $\mu = \sqrt{3}$
2. $\Rightarrow$ Here, angle of incidence $\Rightarrow i = \tan^{-1}(\mu)$
3. Hence, reflected and refracted rays would be perpendicular to each other.
solution.html:
1. Given i = 60° and μ = 3
  2. ⇒ Here, angle of incidence ⇒ i = tan-1(μ)
  3. Hence, reflected and refracted rays would be perpendicular to each other.
steps: Given $i = 60^\circ$ and $\mu = \sqrt{3}$
$\Rightarrow$ Here, angle of incidence $\Rightarrow i = \tan^{-1}(\mu)$
Hence, reflected and refracted rays would be perpendicular to each other.
printed_lines: Here, angle of incidence  i = tan^{–1}()
Hence, reflected and refracted rays would be perpendicular to each other.

steps: Snell's law: $\sin 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\,\sin r$.
$\sin r = \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{2}$, so $r = 30^\circ$.
The reflected ray makes $60^\circ$ with the normal on the incident side; the refracted ray makes $30^\circ$ with the normal on the other side.
Angle between them $= 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 30^\circ = 90^\circ$, which is option $4$ (consistent with Brewster's law, $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$).
ai_solution.html:
1. Snell's law: sin 60° = 3 sin r.
  2. sin r = 3/23 = 12, so r = 30°.
  3. The reflected ray makes 60° with the normal on the incident side; the refracted ray makes 30° with the normal on the other side.
  4. Angle between them = 180° - 60° - 30° = 90°, which is option 4 (consistent with Brewster's law, tan 60° = 3).
ai_solution.why: sin60/sin r = sqrt3 gives r = 30 deg; angle between reflected and refracted rays = 180 - 60 - 30 = 90 deg (Brewster incidence, tan60 = sqrt3).

chapter.name: Ray Optics

subtopics.name: Snell's Law
subtopics.why: The answer depends on applying Snell's law (sin 60° = √3 sin r gives r = 30°), so the reflected ray at 60° and refracted ray at 30° are 90° apart.

step_list: Apply Snell's law: sin 60° / sin r = √3, giving sin r = 1/2
Get refraction angle r = 30°, and note the reflected ray leaves at 60° on the other side of the normal
Use the straight-surface geometry: angle between refracted and reflected rays = 180° − (60° + 30°)
difficulty.why: Three short steps but each distractor is a genuine partial result of the same calculation — the refraction angle, the reflection angle and the 180°−2i slip — so elimination does nothing and only carrying the geometry through to the end separates them; the computation itself is light, which keeps it off the hard end.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Every wrong option is an intermediate quantity of the correct working, so a candidate who stops one step early lands exactly on a printed option rather than on nothing.

source.note: Text draft rendered the radical as plain '3'; image clearly shows $\sqrt{3}$.

chapter.why: The answer depends on conservation of mass number and charge in beta-plus decay, giving the daughter nucleus ^22_10Ne, which is nuclear radioactive decay.

subtopics.name: Alpha, Beta, and Gamma Decay
subtopics.why: The answer depends on beta-plus decay lowering the atomic number by one while keeping the mass number unchanged, so 22/11 Na becomes 22/10 Ne.

step_list: Balance mass number: 22 = A + 0 + 0, so X has A = 22, which already rules out the two mass-23 options.
Balance charge, remembering the emitted particle is a positron (+1): 11 = Z + 1, so Z = 10, i.e. the proton has turned into a neutron and Z drops.
difficulty.why: Two short conservation checks, but the band is set by the options rather than the arithmetic: the mass-number step kills half the list, and the surviving pair Mg-22 / Ne-22 is a deliberate sign trap that only correctly reading the e+ superscript resolves.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Everything turns on one superscript — the '+' on the emitted electron. A skimming candidate reads 'beta decay', raises Z by one and lands precisely on option 1; nothing else in the stem flags the direction of the charge change.

(1) $9 : 4$
(2) $1 : 4$
(3) $4 : 1$
(4) $4 : 9$

  1. (1)9 : 4

  3. (3)4 : 1
  4. (4)4 : 9
question.stem: Let $T_1$ and $T_2$ be the energy of an electron in the first and second excited states of hydrogen atoms, respectively. According to the Bohr's model of an atom, the ratio $T_1 : T_2$ is

solution.full_text:
1. $E_n = \frac{E_0}{n^2}$, For first excited state $\Rightarrow n = 2$
2. For second excited state $\Rightarrow n = 3$
3. $\Rightarrow \frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{\frac{E_0}{4}}{\frac{E_0}{9}} = \frac{9}{4}$
solution.html:
1. En = E0n2, For first excited state ⇒ n = 2
  2. For second excited state ⇒ n = 3
  3. ⇒ T1T2 = E04E09 = 94
steps: $E_n = \frac{E_0}{n^2}$, For first excited state $\Rightarrow n = 2$
For second excited state $\Rightarrow n = 3$
$\Rightarrow \frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{\frac{E_0}{4}}{\frac{E_0}{9}} = \frac{9}{4}$
The first excited state is $n=2$ and the second excited state is $n=3$.
In Bohr's model $E_n = -\frac{13.6}{n^2}\,\text{eV}$, so $E_n \propto \frac{1}{n^2}$.
$T_1 : T_2 = 9 : 4$, which is option $1$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The first excited state is n=2 and the second excited state is n=3.
  2. In Bohr's model En = -13.6n2 eV, so En ∝ 1n2.
  3. T1T2 = 1/221/32 = 94.
  4. T1 : T2 = 9 : 4, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: First and second excited states are n=2 and n=3; Bohr energy is proportional to 1/n^2, so T1:T2 = (1/4):(1/9) = 9:4.

solution.full_text:

2. Tensile strength of steel is more than that of copper.

spec.title: Two NAND gates (one input of the lower one through a NOT gate) feeding an AND gate with output C

steps: From the figure, the top NAND gate takes inputs $A$ and $B$, so its output is $\overline{AB}$.
The bottom NAND gate takes $\bar{A}$ (through the NOT gate) and $B$, so its output is $\overline{\bar{A}B}$.
The AND gate gives $C = \overline{AB}\cdot\overline{\bar{A}B} = (\bar{A}+\bar{B})(A+\bar{B})$.
$(\bar{A}+\bar{B})(A+\bar{B}) = \bar{B} + A\bar{A} = \bar{B}$.
So $C = 1, 0, 1, 0$ for $AB = 00, 01, 10, 11$, which is option $4$.
ai_solution.html:
1. From the figure, the top NAND gate takes inputs A and B, so its output is AB.
  2. The bottom NAND gate takes A (through the NOT gate) and B, so its output is AB.
  3. The AND gate gives C = AB·AB = (A+B)(A+B).
  4. (A+B)(A+B) = B + AA = B.
  5. So C = 1, 0, 1, 0 for AB = 00, 01, 10, 11, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: C = (AB)' . (A'B)' which simplifies to B', giving C = 1,0,1,0 for AB = 00,01,10,11.

steps: Light is slower in $A$ ($1.5 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$) than in $B$ ($2.0 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$), so $A$ is the denser medium and total internal reflection happens for light going from $A$ to $B$.
$\sin C = \frac{n_B}{n_A}$.
$\frac{n_B}{n_A} = \frac{c/v_B}{c/v_A} = \frac{v_A}{v_B}$.
$C = \sin^{-1}(0.750)$, which is option $3$.

  2. sin C = nBnA.
  3. nBnA = c/vBc/vA = vAvB.
  4. sin C = 1.5 × 1082.0 × 108 = 0.750.
  5. C = sin-1(0.750), which is option 3.
ai_solution.why: Light is slower in A, so A is denser; sin C = n_B/n_A = v_A/v_B = 1.5/2.0 = 0.75.

steps: For solid wire
Inside point
$B = \frac{\mu_0 I r^2}{R^2 \times 2\pi r}$
$= \frac{\mu_0 I r}{R^2 \times 2\pi}$
$B \propto r$
Outside point

For $r < R$, the enclosed current is $I_{enc} = I\frac{r^2}{R^2}$ (uniform current density).

question.stem: Two pendulums of length $121\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $100\,\mathrm{cm}$ start vibrating in phase. At some instant, the two are at their mean position in the same phase. The minimum number of vibrations of the shorter pendulum after which the two are again in phase at the mean position is:

solution.full_text:
1. $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$
2. Let $n_1$ and $n_2$ be integer.
3. $n_1 T_1 = n_2 T_2$
4. $2\pi n_1\sqrt{\frac{1.21}{g}} = 2\pi n_2\sqrt{\frac{1.00}{g}}$
5. $\Rightarrow \frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{11}{10}$
6. $\therefore$ After completion of $11^{\mathrm{th}}$ oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.

  2. Let n1 and n2 be integer.
  3. n1 T1 = n2 T2
  4. 2π n11.21g = 2π n21.00g
  5. ⇒ n2n1 = 1110
  6. ∴ After completion of 11th oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.
steps: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$
Let $n_1$ and $n_2$ be integer.
$2\pi n_1\sqrt{\frac{1.21}{g}} = 2\pi n_2\sqrt{\frac{1.00}{g}}$

After completion of 11^{th} oscillation of shorter pendulum, it will be in phase with longer pendulum.

steps: For a simple pendulum $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}$, so $T \propto \sqrt{l}$.
$\frac{T_{long}}{T_{short}} = \sqrt{\frac{121}{100}} = \frac{11}{10}$.
They are again in phase at the mean position when $n\,T_{short} = m\,T_{long}$ for whole numbers $n, m$.
$n\,T_{short} = m \cdot \frac{11}{10} T_{short} \Rightarrow 10n = 11m$.
The smallest whole-number solution is $n = 11$, $m = 10$, so the shorter pendulum makes $11$ vibrations, which is option $2$.

  2. TlongTshort = 121100 = 1110.
  3. They are again in phase at the mean position when n Tshort = m Tlong for whole numbers n, m.
  4. n Tshort = m · 1110 Tshort ⇒ 10n = 11m.
  5. The smallest whole-number solution is n = 11, m = 10, so the shorter pendulum makes 11 vibrations, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: T is proportional to sqrt(l), so T_long/T_short = 11/10; they are next in phase when n*T_short = m*T_long, smallest n = 11.

solution.full_text:

2. Thermosetting polymers are cross-linked or heavily branched molecules, which on heating undergo extensive cross-linking in moulds and again become infusible. These cannot be reused.

4. Fibres possess high tensile strength.

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{CH_3COONa} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}$, $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}(\mathrm{p}K_a) = 4.57$
2. $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$        $0.01\,\mathrm{M}$

6. $= 4.57 + \log\left(\frac{0.1}{0.01}\right)$
7. $= 4.57 + 1$
8. $= 5.57$

  6. = 4.57 + log(0.10.01)
  7. = 4.57 + 1

steps: Sodium acetate with acetic acid forms an acidic buffer, so $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$.
Equal volumes ($50\,\mathrm{mL}$ each) are mixed, so the ratio is $\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]} = \frac{0.10}{0.01} = 10$.
$\mathrm{pH} = 4.57 + \log 10 = 4.57 + 1 = 5.57$, which is option $2$.

steps: Gd ($Z=64$) has configuration $[\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7 5d^1 6s^2$.
After two ionisations, $\mathrm{Gd^{2+}} = [\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7 5d^1$.
The third ionisation removes the $5d^1$ electron, giving $\mathrm{Gd^{3+}} = [\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7$, a half-filled $4f$ subshell.
The half-filled $4f^7$ state is stabilised by high exchange enthalpy, so $\Delta_i H_3$ is low, which is option $3$.

solution.full_text:

3. $\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell} = E^{o}_{cathode} - E^{o}_{anode}}$
4. $= -0.44\,\mathrm{V} - (-0.76\,\mathrm{V})$
5. $= 0.32\,\mathrm{V}$
6. For, $\mathrm{2CuSO_4(aq) + 2Ag(s) \rightarrow 2Cu(s) + Ag_2SO_4(aq)}$
7. $\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}} = 0.34\,\mathrm{V} - 0.80\,\mathrm{V}$
8. $= -0.46\,\mathrm{V}$
9. For, $\mathrm{CuSO_4(aq) + Zn(s) \rightarrow ZnSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)}$
10. $\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}} = 0.34\,\mathrm{V} - (-0.76\,\mathrm{V})$
11. $= 1.1\,\mathrm{V}$
12. For, $\mathrm{CuSO_4(aq) + Fe(s) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)}$
13. $\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}} = 0.80\,\mathrm{V} - (-0.44\,\mathrm{V})$
14. $= 1.24\,\mathrm{V}$

solution.full_text:
1. Let m gram mass of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ is required
2. Pure $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in m gram $= \frac{95}{100} \times \mathrm{m}$
3. Moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_3} = \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{\mathrm{m}}{100}$
4. Moles of $\mathrm{HCl}$ required $= 2 \times$ moles of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$
5. $= 2 \times \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{\mathrm{m}}{100}$
6. $2 \times \frac{95}{100} \times \frac{\mathrm{m}}{100} = \frac{50}{1000} \times 0.5$
7. $\mathrm{m} = 1.315\,\mathrm{g} \approx 1.32\,\mathrm{g}$

solution.full_text:
1. $\mathrm{Ni(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\,(0.001\,\mathrm{M}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\,(0.001\,\mathrm{M}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}$
2. $\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = 10.5\,\mathrm{V}$
3. $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{cell}} = \mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log\frac{\left[\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\right]^{2}}$
4. $= 10.5 - \frac{0.059}{2}\log\frac{\left(10^{-3}\right)}{\left(10^{-3}\right)^{2}}$
5. $\Rightarrow 10.5 - \frac{0.059}{2}\log\left(10\right)^{3}$
6. $\Rightarrow 10.5 - 0.0295 \times 3$
7. $= 10.5 - 0.0885$
8. $= 10.4115\,\mathrm{V}$
solution.html:
1. Ni(s) + 2Ag+ (0.001 M) → Ni2+ (0.001 M) + 2Ag(s)
  2. E°cell = 10.5 V
  3. Ecell = E°cell - 0.059nlog[Ni2+][Ag+]2
  4. = 10.5 - 0.0592log(10-3)(10-3)2
  5. ⇒ 10.5 - 0.0592log(10)3
  6. ⇒ 10.5 - 0.0295 × 3
  7. = 10.5 - 0.0885
  8. = 10.4115 V
steps: $\mathrm{Ni(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\,(0.001\,\mathrm{M}) \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\,(0.001\,\mathrm{M}) + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}$

$\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{cell}} = \mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{n}\log\frac{\left[\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\right]^{2}}$
$\Rightarrow 10.5 - \frac{0.059}{2}\log\left(10\right)^{3}$
$\Rightarrow 10.5 - 0.0295 \times 3$
The reaction transfers $n = 2$ electrons.
$\log Q = 3$.
$E = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} - \frac{0.059}{2}\log Q = 10.5 - 0.0295 \times 3$.
No option equals $10.4115\,\mathrm{V}$, so no option matches.

  2. Q = [Ni2+][Ag+]2 = 0.001(0.001)2 = 103.
  3. log Q = 3.
  4. E = E°cell - 0.0592log Q = 10.5 - 0.0295 × 3.
  5. E = 10.5 - 0.0885 = 10.4115 V.

question.full_text:
If radius of second Bohr orbit of the $\mathrm{He^{+}}$ ion is $105.8\,\mathrm{pm}$, what is the radius of third Bohr orbit of $\mathrm{Li^{2+}}$ ion?
(1) $158.7\,\mathrm{\AA}$
(2) $158.7\,\mathrm{pm}$
(3) $15.87\,\mathrm{pm}$
(4) $1.587\,\mathrm{pm}$
question.html:
If radius of second Bohr orbit of the He+ ion is 105.8 pm, what is the radius of third Bohr orbit of Li2+ ion?
  1. (1)158.7 Å
  2. (2)158.7 pm
  3. (3)15.87 pm
  4. (4)1.587 pm
question.stem: If radius of second Bohr orbit of the $\mathrm{He^{+}}$ ion is $105.8\,\mathrm{pm}$, what is the radius of third Bohr orbit of $\mathrm{Li^{2+}}$ ion?

solution.html:
1. rn ∝ n2Z
  2. r3(Li2+)r2(He+) = (n3)2Z(Li2+) × Z(He+)(n2)2
  3. r3(Li2+)105.8 = (3)23 × 2(2)2
  4. = 105.8 × 32
  5. r3(Li2+) = 158.7 pm
steps: $r_n \propto \frac{n^2}{Z}$
$\frac{r_3(\mathrm{Li^{2+}})}{r_2(\mathrm{He^{+}})} = \frac{(n_3)^2}{Z(\mathrm{Li^{2+}})} \times \frac{Z(\mathrm{He^{+}})}{(n_2)^2}$
$r_3(\mathrm{Li^{2+}}) = 158.7\,\mathrm{pm}$
Bohr radius formula: $r_n = 0.529\,\text{Å} \times \frac{n^2}{Z}$, i.e. $r_n = 52.9\,\text{pm} \times \frac{n^2}{Z}$.
Verify with He$^+$ ($Z=2$, $n=2$): $r = 52.9 \times \frac{4}{2} = 105.8\,\text{pm}$, matches given data.
This matches option 2.
ai_solution.html:
1. Bohr radius formula: rn = 0.529 Å × n2Z, i.e. rn = 52.9 pm × n2Z.
  2. Verify with He+ (Z=2, n=2): r = 52.9 × 42 = 105.8 pm, matches given data.
  3. For Li2+ (Z=3, n=3): r = 52.9 × 93 = 52.9 × 3 = 158.7 pm.
  4. This matches option 2.
ai_solution.why: Bohr radius scales as n²/Z; using the given He+ value to calibrate, Li2+ (n=3, Z=3) gives 158.7 pm.

solution.html: 1. 1-bromo-5-chloro-4-methylhexan-3-ol
steps: 1-bromo-5-chloro-4-methylhexan-3-ol
The longest chain containing $\ce{-OH}$ runs from the $\ce{CH2Br}$ carbon to the terminal $\ce{CH3}$ next to $\ce{CHCl}$: $6$ carbons, so the parent is hexan-ol.
Numbering from the Br end puts $\ce{-OH}$ at $C_3$; from the other end it would be $C_4$, so number from the Br end.
Substituents then sit at: Br on $C_1$, $\ce{CH3}$ on $C_4$, Cl on $C_5$.
Prefixes in alphabetical order: bromo, chloro, methyl $\Rightarrow$ 1-bromo-5-chloro-4-methylhexan-3-ol, which is option $2$.
ai_solution.html:
1. The longest chain containing -OH runs from the CH2Br carbon to the terminal CH3 next to CHCl: 6 carbons, so the parent is hexan-ol.
  2. Numbering from the Br end puts -OH at C3; from the other end it would be C4, so number from the Br end.
  3. Substituents then sit at: Br on C1, CH3 on C4, Cl on C5.
  4. Prefixes in alphabetical order: bromo, chloro, methyl ⇒ 1-bromo-5-chloro-4-methylhexan-3-ol, which is option 2.
ai_solution.why: Six-carbon chain numbered from the Br end gives OH the lowest locant (4); substituents alphabetical: bromo, chloro, methyl -> 1-bromo-5-chloro-4-methylhexan-3-ol.

subtopics.why: The answer depends on numbering the chain so the principal functional group (-OH, suffix -ol) gets the lowest locant and citing the bromo, chloro and methyl prefixes alphabetically.

step_list: Read the skeleton from the drawing: CH3-CH(Cl)-CH(CH3)-CH(OH)-CH2-CH2-Br, a six-carbon parent chain
Identify -OH as the principal characteristic group, so the suffix is -ol and it takes the lowest locant
Number from the bromomethyl end: C1 Br, C3 OH, C4 CH3, C5 Cl (numbering the other way puts OH at 4, which is higher)
Write the substituent prefixes in alphabetical order: bromo, chloro, methyl
difficulty.why: Hard: four short steps, and three of the four options survive casual inspection because the question tests two independent rules at once — lowest locant to the OH (separating 2/4 from 1/3) and alphabetical ordering of prefixes (separating 2 from 4) — so a candidate who gets the numbering right can still land on option 4.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: Two nomenclature rules joined in one item, with each distractor failing only one of them; the alphabetical-order distractor is semantically identical to the key except for word order and is very easy to tick.

steps: $\mathrm{LiAlH_4}$ then $\mathrm{H_2O}$ reduces the nitrile: $\mathrm{C_6H_5CN \rightarrow C_6H_5CH_2NH_2}$ (benzylamine).

  2. NaNO2 + HCl forms HNO2, which diazotises the primary aliphatic amine: C6H5CH2NH2 → C6H5CH2N2+Cl-.

chapter.name: Amines
chapter.why: The correct answer depends on knowing that the nitrile is reduced to a primary aliphatic amine (benzylamine) which, with HNO2, gives an unstable diazonium that hydrolyses to benzyl alcohol — the reaction of amines with nitrous acid.

subtopics.name: Chemical Reactions of Amines (Carbylamine, Nitrous Acid, Arylsulphonyl Chloride and Electrophilic Substitution Reactions)
subtopics.why: The answer (benzyl alcohol) depends on benzonitrile being reduced by LiAlH4 to benzylamine, a primary aliphatic amine that reacts with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl) to give an unstable diazonium salt which hydrolyses to the alcohol.

subtopics.name: Methods of Preparation of Amines
subtopics.why: Step (i) of the sequence, LiAlH4 reduction of benzonitrile to benzylamine, is a method of preparing amines, and getting that intermediate right is what makes the later nitrous acid step give a benzylic alcohol.

step_list: Recognise LiAlH4 reduces the nitrile to a primary amine — benzylamine (PhCH2NH2), not to an aldehyde or amide.
Treat benzylamine with NaNO2/HCl: diazotisation gives a benzyl diazonium ion, which — being aliphatic — is not isolable and loses N2 immediately.

Decide the fate of the resulting benzyl cation in aqueous medium: water captures it to give benzyl alcohol (the NCERT line is that aliphatic diazonium salts decompose to alcohols with brisk N2 evolution).
difficulty.why: Three linked transformations, each with a standard wrong turn, and three of the four options sit at the end of a real route — the diazonium salt and the benzyl chloride are both one small slip away, so elimination gives nothing and the candidate must carry the whole sequence through.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The unsignposted point is that aliphatic (benzylic) diazonium salts are unstable while aryl ones are isolable; option 3 is the trend-following answer and only that single NCERT caveat rules it out, with option 4 testing whether the nucleophile is Cl⁻ or the water of step (iii).

subtopics.why: The answer depends on which self- and cross-aldol condensation products acetone and 2-pentanone can form with dilute NaOH and heat, an alpha-hydrogen reaction.

step_list: Recognise dilute NaOH + heat on a ketone mixture = crossed aldol condensation giving α,β-unsaturated ketones (aldol then dehydration).
List the enolates available: acetone's CH3, 2-pentanone's C1 methyl, and 2-pentanone's C3 methylene (ethyl-bearing carbon).
List the two electrophilic carbonyls (acetone C=O with two methyls; 2-pentanone C=O with methyl + propyl).
Build the six possible cross/self condensation products and note which acyl fragments can survive: only CH3CO- and CH3CH2CH2CO-, never CH3CH2CO-.
Decode each of the four drawn skeletons (count the chain on each side of the C=C and the carbonyl) and find the one whose acyl group or carbon skeleton cannot arise.
difficulty.why: Hard: five steps of enumeration plus the slow visual work of parsing four condensed line structures from the image, and elimination gives no help at all because every option is a plausible condensation product — only a candidate who notices that a propanoyl (CH3CH2CO-) fragment can never arise from acetone or 2-pentanone gets there.
difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: A 'not formed' stem over a crossed aldol with three distinct enolates — the candidate must generate the whole product set rather than check one reaction, and the trap is forgetting the C3 enolate of 2-pentanone (which makes option 1 look wrong) or misreading a drawn ethyl for a propyl.

solution.html:

  4. = 8.92 × 6.023 × 1023 × (3.608 × 10-8)34
  5. = 8.92 × 6.023 × 1023 × 46.97 × 10-244 = 2523.47 × 10-14

steps: $d = \frac{ZM}{N_A (a)^3}$

5. $[\mathrm{O_3}] = 4.38 \times 10^{-32}$

  4. [O3]2 = 1.9 × 10-63 = 19 × 10-64
  5. [O3] = 4.38 × 10-32
  6. Concentration of O3 at equilibrium = 4.38 × 10-32 M

steps: A restriction enzyme recognises a palindromic sequence, one that reads the same on both strands in the $5' \to 3'$ direction.
Option 3: top $5'\mathrm{GAATTC}3'$; bottom read $5' \to 3'$ is $\mathrm{GAATTC}$, so it is palindromic and is the EcoRI recognition site.
Options 2, 4, 1: bottom strands read $5' \to 3'$ are $\mathrm{AGTATC}$, $\mathrm{TGACTC}$, $\mathrm{GAATAC}$, which differ from the top strands, so they are not palindromes.

  4. Hence the answer is option 3.
ai_solution.why: GAATTC/CTTAAG reads the same 5' to 3' on both strands (true palindrome) and is the EcoRI recognition site; the other sequences are not palindromic.

5. Spermatogenesis is a continuous process that begins at puberty. So (e) is true for spermatogenesis. Oogenesis on the other hand begins during embryonic development of the female.

(b) Spermatids differentiate into sperms (spermiogenesis) after meiosis is complete; in oogenesis meiosis II finishes only after sperm entry, so (b) applies to spermatogenesis only.
(c) Spermatogonia form a mitotically dividing stem-cell population that keeps entering meiosis; oogonia stop multiplying before birth, so (c) applies to spermatogenesis only.

step_list: Check (a): haploid gametes result from both spermatogenesis and oogenesis — shared, so reject.

Check (b): in spermatogenesis spermiogenesis (differentiation) follows completed meiosis, whereas the oocyte grows/differentiates while still arrested in meiosis I and finishes meiosis II only after fertilisation — spermatogenesis only.
Check (c): spermatogonia remain a continuously mitotically dividing stem-cell pool feeding meiosis, while oogonia stop multiplying before birth — spermatogenesis only.
Check (d): both processes are driven by anterior-pituitary LH and FSH — shared, reject.
Check (e): spermatogenesis begins at puberty, oogenesis begins in foetal life — spermatogenesis only; combine (b), (c), (e).

(1) RNA polymerase will bind the promoter region
(2) Only z gene will get transcribed
(3) z, y, a genes will be transcribed
(4) z, y, a genes will not be translated

  2. (2)Only z gene will get transcribed
  3. (3)z, y, a genes will be transcribed
  4. (4)z, y, a genes will not be translated
question.stem: In an E. Coli strain i gene gets mutated and its product can not bind the inducer molecule. If growth medium is provided with lactose, what will be the outcome?

options.text: RNA polymerase will bind the promoter region
Only z gene will get transcribed
z, y, a genes will be transcribed
z, y, a genes will not be translated

answer.publisher_text: z, y, a genes will not be translated
answer.ai_text: z, y, a genes will not be translated

solution.full_text:
1. As the product of '$i$' gene binds with the operator region and blocks the transcription and translation of $z$, $y$ and $a$ genes.
2. It's product is prevented from binding to the operator by attaching it with the inducer. As the inducer can now no more capable of binding with the repressor, thus, in all the cases, operator always gets attached with the repressor thereby preventing the transcription and transmission of $z$, $y$ and $a$.
3. Even in the presence of lactose, transcription and translation of $z$, $y$ and $a$ would not occur.

steps: Recombination frequency is proportional to map distance, so the farthest pair $a$–$d$ ($29\%$) are the two ends.
$a$–$c = 5\%$ is smallest from $a$, so $c$ lies next to $a$: $a, c, \dots$
$c$–$b = 15\%$ places $b$ after $c$: $a$–$b = 5 + 15 = 20\%$, matching the given value.
$b$–$d = 9\%$ places $d$ last: $c$–$d = 15 + 9 = 24\%$ and $a$–$d = 5 + 15 + 9 = 29\%$, both matching.
The order is $a, c, b, d$, which is option $1$.

  4. b–d = 9% places d last: c–d = 15 + 9 = 24% and a–d = 5 + 15 + 9 = 29%, both matching.
  5. The order is a, c, b, d, which is option 1.
ai_solution.why: Distances are additive along the order a-c-b-d: a-c 5, c-b 15, b-d 9 give a-b 20, c-d 24, a-d 29, all matching.

steps: E. coli divides once every $20\,\text{min}$, so in $60\,\text{min}$ there are $\frac{60}{20} = 3$ generations.
Total cells after 3 generations: $10 \times 2^3 = 80$.
Replication is semiconservative: the two original $^{15}N$ strands of each parent DNA stay intact and end up in 2 cells, so cells carrying $^{15}N$ $= 10 \times 2 = 20$.
Cells totally free of $^{15}N$ $= 80 - 20 = 60$, which is option $4$.

  2. Total cells after 3 generations: 10 × 23 = 80.
  3. Replication is semiconservative: the two original 15N strands of each parent DNA stay intact and end up in 2 cells, so cells carrying 15N = 10 × 2 = 20.
  4. Cells totally free of 15N = 80 - 20 = 60, which is option 4.
ai_solution.why: E. coli divides every 20 min, so 3 generations in 60 min give 80 cells; semiconservative replication leaves 20 hybrid cells, so 60 cells are free of 15N.

ai_solution.html:
1. Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide in animals, so (a) → (iv).
  2. Globulins (immunoglobulins) function as antibodies, so (b) → (iii).
  3. Steroids such as testosterone and oestrogen act as hormones, so (c) → (i).
  4. Thrombin is an enzyme in blood clotting, i.e. a biocatalyst, so (d) → (ii).
  5. The match a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii is option 1.

difficulty.what_makes_it_hard: The near-neighbour trap: globulin and thrombin are both plasma proteins, and option 3 is built by swapping just those two, so recognising the familiar NCERT table is not enough — the candidate must know thrombin is specifically an enzyme.
